newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Why do Franz and Fritz give Vienna stocks a miss?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Why do Franz and Fritz give Vienna stocks a miss?.

text.p: If you throw a stone into a crowd of Austrians, the odds on hitting someone called Franz or Fritz are very high.
But landing a shot on an Austrian who invests in stocks is next to impossible.
Austria is the world's second lowest stock investor at just four percent of the population, with only India coming in lower at two percent.

This wealthy nation's antipathy towards stocks has its roots firmly in history. Many Austrians still remember the poverty and hunger they experienced after Austria was defeated in both world wars, wiping out life savings and sending unemployment and inflation sky-high.

"Austrians are very conservative investors, choosing rather to put their money into building savings schemes or savings accounts where there is minimal risk," said Odilo Seisser, of market research institute Fessel-GfK in Vienna.
"People lost their money twice so they've basically become very conservative," said Gerhard Reidlinger, spokesman for the Vienna stock exchange.
PROPERTY BEATS STOCKS FOR SECURITY
The Beck family is a case in point. When the father Johann, who owned a liquor distillery in Vienna, died in 1910 he left his three daughters a sizeable inheritance.
Two daughters invested their share in Vienna appartment blocks and land, and the third turned to the stock market.

But following Austria's defeat in World War One, the latter saw her investment totally wiped out, while the daughters with real estate saw the value of their holdings surge as workers moved into Vienna from the provinces in search of work.

The low level of stock investment has been stagnant for decades in Austria. Neighbouring Germany is also low at around seven percent, as is Japan, while every fifth American buys stocks and every third Swede.
History has also left its scars on life insurance companies and pension funds -- traditionally the largest investors in financial markets. The bulk of their portfolio is in fixed income.
Austrian law allows pension funds to invest up to 40 percent in the stock market, and 30 percent for insurance companies. But none comes close to investing that much.
The Alpine republic's largest insurance group EA-Generali last year invested around eight percent of its portfolio in stocks.

The Vienna stock exchange, one of the world's oldest and established in 1771 by Empress Maria Theresia to service the wealth generated by the Austro-Hungarian Empire, is often ridiculed as a banana republic exchange due to the lack of companies on offer and low liquidity.
The exchange's blue-chip ATX index consists of just 21 stocks -- and arguably only a handful can truly be labelled blue chips. In total, 105 companies are listed on the stock exchange.
BANKRUPTCIES AND A BAD PRESS DETER
A lack of insight into the stock market combined with recent high-profile bankruptcies further discourage the average Austrian in the street from dabbling in stocks.

A bad press has also taken its toll. The exchange suffered a barrage of fire when building group Maculan went bankrupt last year, becoming the biggest failure of an Austrian listed company since World War Two.

Critics say the bourse's lax regulations and leaky supervision enabled Maculan to flout stock exchange rules. The exchange fined Maculan a mere 100,000 schillings ($8,150) for breaching disclosure rules when it abandoned an upbeat profit forecast for a considerable loss.
Vienna bowed to world pressure last year to abolish its anonymous securities accounts to clamp down on money laundering and insider trading. Insider trading only became illegal in Austria in 1993.
HIGH BUY AND SELL FEES DISCOURAGE

Exorbitant fees involved with stock investment hardly win over the tentative investor. Each transaction, be it a buy or sell order, costs the investor on average 1.25 percent of the share price compared to 0.6 percent in Germany.

But despite the many obstacles, individual investors may be kicking themselves for shunning stocks, having missed out on some spectacular share price gains over the last 18 months while interest rates have trickled down to a historic low.

Semperit, a rubber products maker, has surged over 400 percent, BWT, a maker of water-treatment technology, nearly 80 percent, while engineering group VA Tech, probably Austria's most international company, has gained 70 percent.

The Vienna Bourse, painfully aware it needs brush up its image and strengthen Vienna's position in an increasingly competitive European market, has introduced a new market segment called Fit to encourage smaller and medium-sized firms to list their shares.
And the bourse last July introduced a new electronic quote and order driven system (EQOS) in an attempt to boost liquidity and attract more foreign investors.
"I think all these measures will have an impact in the medium term on the confidence of the investor," said the bourse's Reidlinger.
